claim: Id2 is a potent binding partner of active Akt based on proteomic analysis in PC12 cells.
source: Interestingly, our proteomic analysis showed that Id2 is a potent binding partner of active Akt (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which displays silver staining results from PC12 cells transfected with constitutively active (CA) or kinase-dead (KD) forms of Akt.

claim: Endogenous interaction occurs between Akt and Id2 in mouse brain lysates.
source: Indeed, we found endogenous interaction between Akt and Id2 in mouse brain lysates (Figure 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1A using mouse brain lysates.

claim: Among the three Akt isoforms (Akt1-3), Id2 interacts specifically with Akt1.
source: Employing Flag-tagged Akt isoforms (Akt1-3), we verified that, among the three isoforms evaluated, Id2 interacts with Akt1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1C using Flag-tagged Akt isoforms.

claim: The PH domain of Akt interacts with Id2.
source: Our mapping analysis showed that the PH domain of Akt interacts with Id2 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 1D using Akt domain fragments.

claim: The helix domain of Id2 adjacent to the C-terminus binds to Akt.
source: Reciprocal experiments with a series of purified GST-tagged Id2 fragments demonstrated that the helix domain of Id2 adjacent to the C-terminus bound to Akt (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 1E using Id2 domain fragments.

claim: Among the Id family proteins (Id1-4), only Id2 is substantially phosphorylated by active Akt.
source: Among the Id family proteins, only the Id2 protein was substantially phosphorylated by active Akt, although all Id 1–4 proteins interacted with Akt (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The specific site of Id2 phosphorylation by Akt is located on the N-terminus within amino acid residues 1–37.
source: We verified that the specific site of Id2 phosphorylation by Akt is located on the very end of the N-terminus, within amino acid residues 1–37 (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1G using Id2 fragments.

claim: Serine 14 (S14) on Id2 is the phosphorylation site for Akt.
source: In vitro kinase assay with phospho-ablated mutant forms of Id2, revealed that Id2-S14A completely lacked phosphorylation, whereas WT-Id2 and mutation on Serine 5 of Id2, which has been shown to be phosphorylated by cyclin A/cdk2 (Hara et al., 1994), showed strong phosphorylation by Akt. This finding was in agreement with our phospho-proteomic analysis, which revealed S14 to be a putative phosphorylation site of Akt (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1H and phospho-proteomic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: S14 on Id2 is phosphorylated in primary cultured neurons as they develop.
source: To confirm specific phosphorylation at S14 on Id2, we generated phospho-specific antibody that recognized S14 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E) and demonstrated that S14 is indeed phosphorylated in primary cultured neurons as they develop (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1I using phospho-specific antibody in DIV1-5 cortical neurons.

claim: Id2 was highly expressed in the mouse hippocampus in the embryonic stages (E14 and E17) and decreased after birth and overtime (P7-P28).
source: Id2 was highly expressed in the mouse hippocampus in the embryonic stages (E14 and E17) and decreased after birth and overtime (P7-P28).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A showing Id2 levels at different developmental stages.

claim: The level of phospho-Akt paralleled the decrease in Id2, showing a drastic decrease after P14 in the postnatal hippocampus of mouse brain.
source: The level of phospho-Akt paralleled the decrease in Id2, showing a drastic decrease after P14 in the postnatal hippocampus of mouse brain (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A showing phospho-Akt levels at different developmental stages.

claim: Only the level of Akt1, but not that of Akt2 or Akt3, was reduced in a time frame similar to that of Id2.
source: Only the level of Akt1, but not that of Akt2 or Akt3, was reduced in a time frame similar to that of Id2 (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B showing Akt isoform levels at different developmental stages.

claim: Overexpression of Cdh1 markedly reduced endogenous Id2 level, and this effect was prevented by Akt expression in PC12 cells.
source: Overexpression of Cdh1 markedly reduced endogenous Id2 level; importantly, this effect was prevented by Akt expression in PC12 cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating Id2 protein levels with Cdh1 and Akt overexpression.

claim: In cortical neurons, Id2 protein level was proportionally increased with increased Akt level in the presence of Cdh1.
source: In cortical neurons, Id2 protein level was proportionally increased with increased Akt level in the presence of Cdh1, indicating that Akt prevents Id2 degradation (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2D demonstrating Id2 protein levels with increasing Akt in the presence of Cdh1.

claim: Polyubiquitination of Id2 was efficiently abrogated in the presence, but not in the absence of Akt.
source: Accordingly, polyubiquitination of Id2 was efficiently abrogated in the presence, but not in the absence of Akt (Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2E demonstrating ubiquitinated Id2 levels with and without Akt.

claim: The interaction between Id2 and Cdh1 weakened with increased Akt expression, whereas the interaction of Id2 with Akt increased.
source: Id2 was found to be associated with Cdh1. However, the interaction between Id2 and Cdh1 weakened with increased Akt expression, whereas the interaction of Id2 with Akt increased, suggesting that Akt competes with Cdh1 to bind Id2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2F demonstrating the interaction between Id2, Cdh1, and Akt.

claim: The half-life of Id2 was lower in a phospho-ablated mutant (GFP-S14A) than in GFP-Id2-WT-expressing cells, whereas a phospho-mimetic mutant (GFP-S14D) showed more stable expression after cycloheximide (CHX) treatment.
source: The half-life of Id2 was lower in a phospho-ablated mutant (GFP-S14A) that could not be phosphorylated by Akt than in GFP-Id2-WT-expressing cells, whereas a phospho-mimetic mutant (GFP-S14D) showed more stable expression after cycloheximide (CHX) treatment (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 2G demonstrating Id2 protein stability over time.

claim: The phospho-ablated mutant form of Id2 (S14A) showed enhanced association with Cdh1, while Id2-WT and Id2-S14D rarely bound to Cdh1.
source: While Id2-WT and Id2-S14D rarely bound to Cdh1, the phospho-ablated mutant form of Id2 largely showed enhanced association with Cdh1, reflecting its instability and weak detection (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2H demonstrating the interaction between Id2 mutants and Cdh1.

claim: Id2-WT was more stable in the presence of CA-Akt than in that of KD-Akt, while the Id2-S14A mutant was not stabilized by CA-Akt.
source: Moreover, Id2-WT was found to be more stable in the presence of CA-Akt than in that of KD-Akt, while the Id2-S14A mutant was not stabilized by CA-Akt as it could not be phosphorylated. The protein level of phospho-mimetic Id2-S14D was highly stable regardless of whether CA-Akt or KD-Akt was expressed (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2I demonstrating Id2 protein levels with different Akt forms.

claim: Using Akt inhibitor VIII, a reduction of Id2 protein levels occurred as its phosphorylation decreased upon inhibition of AKT phosphorylation.
source: Furthermore, using Akt inhibitor VIII, a chemical inhibitor of Akt signaling, we showed a reduction of Id2 protein levels as its phosphorylation is decreased upon inhibition of AKT phosphorylation, whereas in the presence of PD184352, a chemical inhibitor of MAPK signaling, Id2 stability or phosphorylation is not altered (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2J demonstrating Id2 protein levels with Akt inhibitor treatment.

claim: In the presence of PD184352, a chemical inhibitor of MAPK signaling, Id2 stability or phosphorylation is not altered.
source: Furthermore, using Akt inhibitor VIII, a chemical inhibitor of Akt signaling, we showed a reduction of Id2 protein levels as its phosphorylation is decreased upon inhibition of AKT phosphorylation, whereas in the presence of PD184352, a chemical inhibitor of MAPK signaling, Id2 stability or phosphorylation is not altered (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2J demonstrating Id2 protein levels with MAPK inhibitor treatment.

claim: Akt has been shown to be predominantly localized at the tip of the axon in developing hippocampal neurons.
source: Akt has been shown to be predominantly localized at the tip of the axon in developing hippocampal neurons (Yan et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2006.

claim: During differentiation of rat hippocampal neurons (up to DIV 5), Id2 and Akt were found in proximal axons, with expression tapering off along the distal axon at DIV2.
source: During differentiation of rat hippocampal neurons (up to in vitro day (DIV) 5), the spatial distributions of Id2 and Akt were visualized not only in the soma, but also prominently in the precursors of axons and dendrites in the early stages of differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, DIV1). Id2 and Akt were found in proximal axons, with expression tapering off along the distal axon (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, DIV2)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The signals of Id2 and Akt were strikingly intense at the distal part of the growing axon with a growth cone and axon branching points in later stages of axon growth (DIV 4-5).
source: however, the signals were strikingly intense at the distal part of the growing axon with a growth cone and axon branching points in later stages of axon growth (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, DIV 4 - 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic expression of Id2-WT led to considerably better axon growth and branching than that of control.
source: Ectopic expression of Id2-WT led to considerably better axon growth and branching than that of control
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C measuring axon length and branching points.

claim: S14D expressing neurons showed more abundant branching and extended length of axon than did the control or Id2-WT expressing neurons.
source: S14D expressing neurons showed more abundant branching and extended length of axon than did the control or Id2-WT expressing neurons, revealing high expression at the tip of axon and branching.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C measuring axon length and branching points.

claim: The phospho-ablated mutant (S14A)-expressing neurons exhibited substantially shorter extent of axon growth and less branching in primary cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: In contrast, the phospho-ablated mutant (S14A)-expressing neurons exhibited substantially shorter extent of axon growth and less branching in primary cultured hippocampal neurons (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: GFP signal was not detected in the axonal tip of S14A expressing neurons despite no alteration of this signal in the soma.
source: Interestingly, we failed to detect GFP signal in the axonal tip of S14A expressing neurons despite no alteration of this signal in the soma, indicating lack of Id2 expression in the growth cone of the growing axon (Figure 3B, third panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Prominent endogenous-Id2 expression occurred in the central domain of growth cone and partially colocalized with phalloidin-labeled F-actin.
source: During the differentiation of hippocampal neurons, we found that prominent endogenous-Id2 expression occurred in the central domain of growth cone and partially colocalized with phalloidin-labeled F-actin
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B and quantification in Figure 4C.

claim: S14-phospho-Id2 was localized on punctate structures all-around of the growth cone area and filopodia, staining strongly in the growth cone leading edge and the peripheral domain.
source: while S14-phospho-Id2 was localized on punctate structures all-around of the growth cone area and filopodia. S14-phospho-Id2 stained strongly in the growth cone leading edge and the peripheral domain, revealing notable co-distribution with phalloidin-labeled F-actin in the growing axon (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A-C and quantification in Figure 4C.

claim: In the early stage (stage 1: DIV 1) both Id2 and S14-phospho-Id2 were observed in the filopodial and lamellipodial structure of the leading margin.
source: In the early stage (stage 1: DIV 1) both Id2 and S14-phospho-Id2 were observed in the filopodial and lamellipodial structure of the leading margin.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: As the axon developed (stage II~III: DIV 2 and 3), Id2 was predominantly detected in the central microtubule-containing zone, demonstrating complete co-localization with beta tubulin.
source: However, as the axon developed (stage II~III: DIV 2 and 3), Id2 was predominantly detected in the central microtubule-containing zone, demonstrating complete co-localization with beta tubulin
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: As the axon developed (stage II~III: DIV 2 and 3), S14-phospho-Id2 displayed a more intense signal at the peripheral-domain of growth cone, where there was relatively less beta tubulin staining.
source: while S14-phospho-Id2 displayed a more intense signal at the peripheral-domain of growth cone, where there was relatively less beta tubulin staining (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: S14-phospho-Id2 is relatively enriched in the tip of the growth cone, with respect to that of Id2, as confirmed by fluorescence intensity analysis.
source: Moreover, quantitative analysis that determined the expression level of Id2 or S14-phospho-Id2 from soma to axonal tip, supported the notion that S14-phospho-Id2 is relatively enriched in the tip of the growth cone, with respect to that of Id2, as confirmed by fluorescence intensity analysis (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence intensity analysis shown in Figure 4F and 4G.

claim: Knockdown of Id2 or treatment of Akt inhibitor diminished the specific signal of S14-phospho-Id2 in the growth cone with abnormal feature of growth cone.
source: Either knockdown of Id2 or treatment of Akt inhibitor diminished the specific signal of S14-phospho-Id2 in the growth cone with abnormal feature of growth cone (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: Endogenous Id2 interacts with the ERM proteins in mouse brain extract (E18).
source: When we used an anti-ERM antibody that recognizes an epitope common to all ERM family members, our immunoprecipitation assay mouse brain extract (E18) showed that endogenous Id2 interacts with the ERM proteins (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Brain extracts immunoprecipitated with anti-S14-phospho-Id2 antibody showed a relatively strong interaction with the ERM proteins compared to the binding affinity of Id2 to ERM.
source: Interestingly, compared to the binding affinity of Id2 to ERM, brain extracts immunoprecipitated with anti-S14-phospho-Id2 antibody showed a relatively strong interaction with the ERM proteins (Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Id2 was concentrated in the central region and in the base of some filopodia, while radixin expression was relatively abundant in the peripheral region.
source: Id2 was concentrated in the central region and in the base of some filopodia, while radixin expression was relatively abundant in the peripheral region (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: S14-phospho-Id2 was highly expressed in the peripheral filopodia, revealing co-distribution with radixin.
source: Intriguingly, S14-phospho-Id2 was highly expressed in the peripheral filopodia, revealing co-distribution with radixin, as confirmed by fluorescence analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Id2-WT interacted with radixin, whereas S14A failed to interact with GST-radixin.
source: To further determine the importance of S14 phosphorylation on Id2 in the binding with radixin, we conducted an in vitro binding assay that demonstrated that Id2-WT interacted with radixin, whereas S14A failed to interact with GST-radixin (Figure 5C)
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Depletion of Akt by shRNA reduced the interaction between Id2 and radixin.
source: and depletion of Akt by shRNA reduced the interaction between Id2 and radixin (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5D and immunoblotting/immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Knockdown of Id2 in the growing axon dramatically disrupted growth cone shape and cytoskeletal organization detected in neurons with reduced radixin levels.
source: Control GFP-expressing lentivirus-infected neurons showed normal growth cone architecture that was visualized with expression of radixin. However, knockdown of Id2 in the growing axon dramatically disrupted growth cone shape and cytoskeletal organization detected in neurons with reduced radixin levels (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Knockdown of Id2 resulted in noticeable reduction of growth cone size and shortening of axon length.
source: Quantitative analysis of neuronal response involving alteration of the growth cone indicated noticeable reduction of growth cone size and shortening of axon length, implicating the importance of Id2 expression in the growth cone formation (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Restoring Id2 signaling in the absence of endogenous Id2 by expressing WT or S14D-Id2 rescued the deregulated axon growth.
source: Accordingly, restoring Id2 signaling in the absence of endogenous Id2 expressing WT or S14D-Id2 rescued the deregulated axon growth. Conversely, RFP-vector control or S14A-Id2 mutant expression failed to rescue the effect of Id2 in the growth cone (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 5G and 5H.

claim: RFP-vector control or S14A-Id2 mutant expression failed to rescue the effect of Id2 in the growth cone.
source: Accordingly, restoring Id2 signaling in the absence of endogenous Id2 expressing WT or S14D-Id2 rescued the deregulated axon growth. Conversely, RFP-vector control or S14A-Id2 mutant expression failed to rescue the effect of Id2 in the growth cone (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 5G and 5H.

claim: Upon treatment of the hippocampal neuron (stage III) with an Akt inhibitor, the number of radixin expressing filopodia was greatly diminished in the axonal growth cone.
source: Upon treatment of the hippocampal neuron (stage III) with an Akt inhibitor, we found that the number of radixin expressing filopodia was greatly diminished in the axonal growth cone.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Following Akt inhibitor treatment, the intensity of radixin staining, as well as the intensity of S14-phospho-Id2 staining, was remarkably lower than that of the control.
source: We also observed that the intensity of radixin staining, as well as the intensity of S14-phospho-Id2 staining, as following the treatment, was remarkably lower than that of the control (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Knockdown of radixin in the growing neuron induced alteration in growth cone morphology and size and reduced the number of filopodia.
source: In addition, knockdown of radixin in the growing neuron induced alteration in growth cone morphology and size and reduced the number of filopodia. This phenomenon parallels the alteration of endogenous S14-phospho-Id2 distribution as a reduction of growth cone (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic expression of GFP-S14D-Id2 in neurons lacking radixin was not able to concretely maintain growth cone size and numbers of process.
source: However, ectopic expression of GFP-S14D-Id2 in neurons lacking radixin was not able to concretely maintain growth cone size and numbers of process (Figure 6D)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Akt-mediated S14 phosphorylation did not enhance transcriptional repression function of Id2 against E47.
source: To verify specific roles Id2 in the axonal growth cone, we have further shown that Akt-mediated Id2 phosphorylation did not enhance transcriptional repression function of Id2 against E47. Akt-mediated S14 phosphorylation did not alter the interaction between Id2 and E47 and both S14D and S14A mutants resulted in a repression of E47-activated luciferase activity similar to Id2-WT (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and luciferase assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: Id2 mutants (S51P or V68P) barely repress E47 transcriptional activity while Id2 WT successfully represses E47-mediated transcription.
source: we demonstrated that although Id2 mutants (S51P or V68P) barely repress E47 transcriptional activity while Id2 WT successfully represses E47-mediated transcription displaying relatively high luciferase activity and the mRNA expression of Nogo receptor, one of well-known downstream gene of E47 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C and 3D.

claim: Akt-mediated phosphorylation mimetic mutation in either S51P (S14D/ S51P) or V68P (S14D/V68P) provoked axon growth and growth cone localization of these mutants (S14D/ S51P or S14D/V68P), and its effect resembled that of Id2 WT in the growth cone.
source: Akt-mediated phosphorylation mimetic mutation in either S51P (S14D/ S51P) or V68P (S14D/V68P) provoked axon growth and growth cone localization of these mutants (S14D/ S51P or S14D/V68P), and its effect resembled that of Id2 WT in the growth cone (Figure 6—figure supplement 3E,F)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E and 3F.

claim: Very few short axons regrew in control virus-infected slices after injury in entorhinal-hippocampus organotypic slice co-culture.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Del Río et al., 1997), very few short axons regrew in control virus-infected slices after injury (Figure 7B left).
evidence: The claim is supported by biocytin tracing data shown in Figure 7B and citation to Del Río et al., 1997.

claim: Both the number and length of the regenerating axons that entered the hippocampus were greatly increased in the AAV2-Id2-WT-infected slices.
source: However, both the number and length of the regenerating axons that entered the hippocampus were greatly increased in the AAV2-Id2-WT-infected slices
evidence: The claim is supported by biocytin tracing and quantification data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Expression of the AAV2-Id2-S14A in the slices resulted in an approximate five-fold decrease in the number of regenerating axons growing into the denervated hippocampus from that of the Id2-WT.
source: whereas expression of the AAV2-Id2-S14A in the slices resulted in an approximate five-fold decrease in the number of regenerating axons growing into the denervated hippocampus from that of the Id2-WT (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by biocytin tracing and quantification data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Id2-S14D infection of the damaged brain slice substantially promoted axon regrowth at an even higher rate than that in the Id2-WT.
source: Notably, Id2-S14D infection of the damaged brain slice substantially promoted axon regrowth at an even higher rate than that in the Id2-WT (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by biocytin tracing and quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: Infection with active Akt expressing adenovirus of the injured region was insufficient to promote notable regrowth of axons without reintroduction of Id2.
source: Without reintroduction of Id2, infection with active Akt expressing adenovirus of the injured region was insufficient to promote notable regrowth of axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by biocytin tracing and quantification data shown in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: Co-infection of active Akt with AAV2-Id2-WT significantly enhanced the length and numbers of regenerating axons.
source: However, co-infection of active Akt with AAV2-Id2-WT significantly enhanced the length and numbers of regenerating axons, suggesting that Id2 functions downstream of Akt, to control axon regrowth (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by biocytin tracing and quantification data shown in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: Applying Akt inhibitor in the presence of AAV2-Id2-WT led to substantially lower axon regrowth than observed in the AAV2-Id2-WT-expressing slice with no inhibitor.
source: In agreement with this finding, applying Akt inhibitor in the presence of AAV2-Id2-WT led to substantially lower axon regrowth than observed in the AAV2-Id2-WT-expressing slice with no inhibitor (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by biocytin tracing and quantification data shown in Figure 7F and 7G.

claim: Akt/PKB signaling controls both axon establishment and elongation both during development and in the regeneration of mature neurons through glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3).
source: In addition to its role in neuronal survival (Ahn et al., 2004b; Ahn and Ye, 2005), Akt/PKB (protein kinase B) signaling controls a variety of neuronal responses. It regulates both axon establishment and elongation both during development and in the regeneration of mature neurons through glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ahn et al., 2004b and Ahn and Ye, 2005.

claim: The mechanism of GSK3 control of peripheral axon regeneration is controversial and its function in CNS axon regeneration remains unknown.
source: However, the mechanism of GSK3 control of peripheral axon regeneration is controversial and its function in CNS axon regeneration remains unknown (Jiang et al., 2005; Yoshimura et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2011; Saijilafu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014; Gobrecht et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Jiang et al., 2005; Yoshimura et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2011; Saijilafu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014; Gobrecht et al., 2014).

claim: Akt links a host of signaling molecules through activation of mTORC1, which regulates cap-dependent protein translation by inhibiting TSC1/2 to allow axon development, growth, and regeneration in CNS.
source: Moreover, Akt links a host of signaling molecules through activation of mTORC1, which regulates cap-dependent protein translation by inhibiting TSC1/2 to allow axon development, growth, and regeneration in CNS (Ma et al., 2008; Li et al., 2008; Morita and Sobue, 2009; Park et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2008; Li et al., 2008; Morita and Sobue, 2009; Park et al., 2008.

claim: Some evidence suggested an mTORC1 independent pathway that regulates axon regrowth in phosphatase and tensin homolog (Pten) deficient neurons.
source: However, some evidence suggested an mTORC1 independent pathway that regulates axon regrowth in phosphatase and tensin homolog (Pten) deficient neurons (Park et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2008 and Yang et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibitor of DNA binding 2 (Id2) is a negative regulator of basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors.
source: Inhibitor of DNA binding 2 (Id2) is a negative regulator of basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Id2 function.

claim: During development, Id2 binds to bHLH transcription factors and hampers their ability to activate transcription of several growth inhibitory molecules and receptors, thus promoting axon growth.
source: During development, Id2 binds to bHLH transcription factors and hampers their ability to activate transcription of several growth inhibitory molecules and receptors, thus promoting axon growth (Jackson, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jackson, 2006.

claim: Id2 degradation by a complex of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome and its activator Cdh1 (APC/CCdh1) reduces axonal growth in the adult.
source: Id2 degradation by a complex of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome and its activator Cdh1 (APC/CCdh1) reduces axonal growth in the adult (Stegmüller and Bonni, 2005; Lasorella et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stegmüller and Bonni, 2005 and Lasorella et al., 2006.

claim: Protection from Id2 degradation results in erratic growth and an abnormal distribution of parallel fibers in the cerebral cortex.
source: Conversely, protection from Id2 degradation results in erratic growth and an abnormal distribution of parallel fibers in the cerebral cortex (Konishi et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Konishi et al., 2004.

claim: Enhanced Id2 expression in the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) promotes axonal growth after spinal cord injury.
source: while enhanced Id2 expression in the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) promotes axonal growth after spinal cord injury (Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2011.

claim: Injured axons of the adult central nervous system (CNS) do not regenerate, because the ability to activate growth genes and growth cone substantially declines as neurons mature.
source: Injured axons of the adult central nervous system (CNS) do not regenerate, because the ability to activate growth genes and growth cone substantially declines as neurons mature (Fawcett, 2001; Fernandes and Tetzlaff, 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fawcett, 2001 and Fernandes and Tetzlaff, 2001.

claim: The CNS environment is hostile to axon regeneration processes.
source: and the CNS environment is hostile to those processes (Filbin, 2006; Goldberg et al., 2002; Silver and Miller, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Filbin, 2006; Goldberg et al., 2002; Silver and Miller, 2004.

claim: Neutralization of environmental inhibition is not sufficient for axon regeneration.
source: Neutralization of environmental inhibition is not sufficient for axon regeneration; therefore, elucidating intrinsic growth capacity and regulation of the neuron after injury is of critical importance (Yiu and He, 2006; Lee et al., 2009; Fawcett et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yiu and He, 2006; Lee et al., 2009; Fawcett et al., 1992.

claim: Recent studies have proposed that reactivation of the intrinsic growth ability promotes CNS axon regeneration.
source: Indeed, recent studies have proposed that reactivation of the intrinsic growth ability promotes CNS axon regeneration (Rossi et al., 2001; Teng and Tang, 2006; Bouquet and Nothias, 2007; Smith et al., 2009; Leibinger et al., 2013; Watkins et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Rossi et al., 2001; Teng and Tang, 2006; Bouquet and Nothias, 2007; Smith et al., 2009; Leibinger et al., 2013; Watkins et al., 2013).

claim: The mechanisms involved in axonal regeneration of the mature CNS have many features in common with those important in CNS development.
source: It has been proposed that the mechanisms involved in axonal regeneration of the mature CNS have many features in common with those important in CNS development (Cui, 2006; Harel and Strittmatter, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cui, 2006 and Harel and Strittmatter, 2006.

claim: ERM proteins link the actin cytoskeleton to the plasma membrane and play prominent roles in growth cone morphology and motility.
source: ERM proteins link the actin cytoskeleton to the plasma membrane and play prominent roles in growth cone morphology and motility (Mangeat et al., 1999; Dickson et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mangeat et al., 1999 and Dickson et al., 2002.

claim: Ezrin and moesin expression is strongest in the central region of growth cone.
source: While ezrin and moesin expression is strongest in the central region of growth cone, radixin is highly stained in the peripheral region with phalloidin-label F-actin (Marsick et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Marsick et al., 2012.

claim: Radixin is highly stained in the peripheral region with phalloidin-label F-actin.
source: While ezrin and moesin expression is strongest in the central region of growth cone, radixin is highly stained in the peripheral region with phalloidin-label F-actin (Marsick et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Marsick et al., 2012.

claim: Serine 5 of Id2 has been shown to be phosphorylated by cyclin A/cdk2.
source: In vitro kinase assay with phospho-ablated mutant forms of Id2, revealed that Id2-S14A completely lacked phosphorylation, whereas WT-Id2 and mutation on Serine 5 of Id2, which has been shown to be phosphorylated by cyclin A/cdk2 (Hara et al., 1994), showed strong phosphorylation by Akt.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hara et al., 1994.

claim: Akt1 mRNA was markedly upregulated in injured neurons in adult rats.
source: It has been reported that Akt1 mRNA was markedly upregulated in injured neurons in adult rats, and that the phosphorylated Akt protein was dramatically increased after axotomy in adult motor neurons (Namikawa et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Namikawa et al., 2000.

claim: Phosphorylated Akt protein was dramatically increased after axotomy in adult motor neurons.
source: It has been reported that Akt1 mRNA was markedly upregulated in injured neurons in adult rats, and that the phosphorylated Akt protein was dramatically increased after axotomy in adult motor neurons (Namikawa et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Namikawa et al., 2000.

claim: Infection with an Id2-adenovirus prevented E47-mediated induction of the Nogo receptor.
source: A recent study has shown that infection with an Id2-adenovirus prevented E47-mediated induction of the Nogo receptor, which is responsible for three myelin proteins (myelin-associated glycoprotein, Nogo-A, and oligodendrocyte myelin glycoprotein) that account for most of the inhibitory activity of CNS myelin (Silver and Miller, 2004; Lasorella et al., 2006; Schwab and Bartholdi, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Silver and Miller, 2004; Lasorella et al., 2006; Schwab and Bartholdi, 1996.

claim: The Nogo receptor is responsible for three myelin proteins (myelin-associated glycoprotein, Nogo-A, and oligodendrocyte myelin glycoprotein) that account for most of the inhibitory activity of CNS myelin.
source: A recent study has shown that infection with an Id2-adenovirus prevented E47-mediated induction of the Nogo receptor, which is responsible for three myelin proteins (myelin-associated glycoprotein, Nogo-A, and oligodendrocyte myelin glycoprotein) that account for most of the inhibitory activity of CNS myelin (Silver and Miller, 2004; Lasorella et al., 2006; Schwab and Bartholdi, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Silver and Miller, 2004; Lasorella et al., 2006; Schwab and Bartholdi, 1996.

claim: Blocking growth inhibitory molecules allowed for limited regeneration.
source: In other studies, blocking growth inhibitory molecules allowed for limited regeneration (Dimou et al., 2006; Fry et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dimou et al., 2006 and Fry et al., 2007.

claim: Akt-mediated phosphorylation of serine 14 (S14) on Id2 enhances Id2 protein stability by means of escape from proteasomal degradation.
source: Here, we discovered that, in the developing neuron from rat, Akt signaling regulates axon growth and growth cone formation through phosphorylation of serine 14 (S14) on Inhibitor of DNA binding 2 (Id2). This enhances Id2 protein stability by means of escape from proteasomal degradation
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data including cycloheximide chase assays (Figure 2G), ubiquitination assays (Figure 2E), and protein stability measurements (Figure 2I).

claim: Akt-mediated phosphorylation of S14 on Id2 steers its localization to the growth cone.
source: This enhances Id2 protein stability by means of escape from proteasomal degradation, and steers its localization to the growth cone, where Id2 interacts with radixin that is critical for growth cone formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing S14-phospho-Id2 localization in growth cones (Figure 4) and the absence of S14A mutant in axonal tips (Figure 3B).

claim: In the growth cone, Id2 interacts with radixin that is critical for growth cone formation.
source: and steers its localization to the growth cone, where Id2 interacts with radixin that is critical for growth cone formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assays (Figure 5C, D) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Knockdown of Id2, or abrogation of Id2 phosphorylation at S14, greatly impairs axon growth and the architecture of growth cone.
source: Knockdown of Id2, or abrogation of Id2 phosphorylation at S14, greatly impairs axon growth and the architecture of growth cone.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data showing reduced axon growth and altered growth cone morphology (Figure 3B, C; Figure 5E, F).

claim: Reinstatement of Akt/Id2 signaling after injury in mouse hippocampal slices redeemed growth promoting ability, leading to obvious axon regeneration.
source: Intriguingly, reinstatement of Akt/Id2 signaling after injury in mouse hippocampal slices redeemed growth promoting ability, leading to obvious axon regeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by biocytin tracing data in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures (Figure 7B-G).

claim: Akt/Id2 signaling is a key module for growth cone formation and axon growth.
source: Our results suggest that Akt/Id2 signaling is a key module for growth cone formation and axon growth, and its augmentation plays a potential role in CNS axonal regeneration.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective experimental data showing the role of Akt/Id2 in axon growth, growth cone formation, and regeneration.

claim: Augmentation of Akt/Id2 signaling plays a potential role in CNS axonal regeneration.
source: Our results suggest that Akt/Id2 signaling is a key module for growth cone formation and axon growth, and its augmentation plays a potential role in CNS axonal regeneration.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing enhanced axon regeneration with AAV2-Id2 infection in injured hippocampal slices (Figure 7).

claim: Akt competes with Cdh1 to bind Id2.
source: Id2 was found to be associated with Cdh1. However, the interaction between Id2 and Cdh1 weakened with increased Akt expression, whereas the interaction of Id2 with Akt increased, suggesting that Akt competes with Cdh1 to bind Id2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that increased Akt expression weakens Id2-Cdh1 interaction while strengthening Id2-Akt interaction (Figure 2F).

claim: Akt regulates Id2 protein stability by preventing APC/CCdh1-mediated degradation.
source: Accordingly, polyubiquitination of Id2 was efficiently abrogated in the presence, but not in the absence of Akt (Figure 2E), indicating that Akt regulates Id2 protein stability by preventing APC/CCdh1-mediated degradation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Akt prevents Id2 ubiquitination (Figure 2E) and that Akt prevents Cdh1-mediated Id2 degradation (Figure 2C, D).

claim: Akt protects Id2 from Cdh1-mediated proteasomal degradation through phosphorylation of Id2.
source: The half-life of Id2 was lower in a phospho-ablated mutant (GFP-S14A) that could not be phosphorylated by Akt than in GFP-Id2-WT-expressing cells, whereas a phospho-mimetic mutant (GFP-S14D) showed more stable expression after cycloheximide (CHX) treatment (Figure 2G). This implies that Akt protects Id2 from Cdh1-mediated proteasomal degradation through phosphorylation of Id2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that phosphorylation status affects Id2 stability (Figure 2G) and interaction with Cdh1 (Figure 2H).

claim: Akt-dependent Id2 phosphorylation enhances resistance to Cdh1-mediated degradation of Id2, interrupting the interaction between Id2 and Cdh1.
source: These data suggest that Akt-dependent Id2 phosphorylation enhances resistance to Cdh1-mediated degradation of Id2, interrupting the interaction between Id2 and Cdh1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple observations including reduced Id2-Cdh1 interaction with Akt (Figure 2F), enhanced Id2 stability with phosphorylation (Figure 2G), and increased Id2-Cdh1 binding with S14A mutant (Figure 2H).

claim: Id2 is potentially a downstream target of Akt in the regulation of axon growth and branching.
source: however, the signals were strikingly intense at the distal part of the growing axon with a growth cone and axon branching points in later stages of axon growth (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, DIV 4 - 5), suggesting that Id2 is potentially a downstream target of Akt in the regulation of axon growth and branching.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-localization of Akt and Id2 at growth cones and branching points (Figure 3A) and the functional data showing Akt-dependent Id2 phosphorylation affects axon growth (Figure 3B, C).

claim: Akt regulates axon growth and branching by regulating Id2 phosphorylation.
source: Taken together, these data imply that Akt regulates axon growth and branching by regulating Id2 phosphorylation and that this phosphorylation is essential for Id2 localization in the growth cone and branching.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that S14D enhances axon growth and branching while S14A impairs it (Figure 3B, C).

claim: S14 phosphorylation of Id2 is essential for Id2 localization in the growth cone and branching.
source: Taken together, these data imply that Akt regulates axon growth and branching by regulating Id2 phosphorylation and that this phosphorylation is essential for Id2 localization in the growth cone and branching.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that S14A mutant fails to localize to axonal tips (Figure 3B) and impairs axon growth and branching (Figure 3C).

claim: S14 phosphorylation probably drives Id2 localization in the peripheral region of growth cone.
source: Thus, our data indicate that S14 phosphorylation of Id2 probably drives its localization in the peripheral region of growth cone.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that S14-phospho-Id2 is enriched in the peripheral region of growth cones (Figure 4B, C) and that knockdown of Id2 or Akt inhibition reduces S14-phospho-Id2 signal in growth cones (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-E).

claim: S14-phospho-Id2 probably binds to radixin among the ERM proteins based on the peripheral distribution of S14-phospho-Id2 and radixin.
source: Interestingly, compared to the binding affinity of Id2 to ERM, brain extracts immunoprecipitated with anti-S14-phospho-Id2 antibody showed a relatively strong interaction with the ERM proteins (Figure 5B), suggesting that S14-phospho-Id2 probably binds to radixin among the ERM proteins based on the peripheral distribution of S14-phospho-Id2 and radixin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-localization of S14-phospho-Id2 and radixin in the peripheral region of growth cones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and the enhanced interaction of S14-phospho-Id2 with ERM proteins (Figure 5B).

claim: Akt-mediated phosphorylation of Id2 is crucial for its association with radixin in the growing axon, which probably contributes to the growth cone function.
source: Hence, Akt-mediated phosphorylation of Id2 is crucial for its association with radixin in the growing axon, which probably contributes to the growth cone function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that S14A fails to bind radixin (Figure 5C), Akt depletion reduces Id2-radixin interaction (Figure 5D), and knockdown of Id2 or radixin disrupts growth cone morphology (Figure 5E, F; Figure 6C).

claim: S14 phosphorylation is critical for the proper function of radixin in the growth cone.
source: We also observed that the intensity of radixin staining, as well as the intensity of S14-phospho-Id2 staining, as following the treatment, was remarkably lower than that of the control (Figure 6A,B). This indicates that S14 phosphorylation is critical for the proper function of radixin in the growth cone.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Akt inhibitor reduces both S14-phospho-Id2 and radixin levels in growth cones (Figure 6A, B).

claim: In addition to transcriptional repression of axonal inhibitory molecules in the nucleus, Id2 expression in the growing axonal growth cone is a decisive factor for normal growth cone formation and axon growth.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that in addition to transcriptional repression of axonal inhibitory molecules in the nucleus (Perk et al., 2005), Id2 expression in the growing axonal growth cone is a decisive factor for normal growth cone formation and axon growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Id2 functions in the growth cone through interaction with radixin (Figure 5, 6) and that this function is independent of transcriptional repression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, 3).

claim: Akt may not simply regulate transcriptional repression of Id2, but also growth cone localization of Id2 that is crucial for its association with radixin in the growing axon.
source: These data also suggest that Akt may not simply regulates transcriptional repression of Id2, but also growth cone localization of Id2 that is crucial for its association with radixin in the growing axon, an association that contributes to growth cone function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that S14 phosphorylation does not affect transcriptional repression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) but is critical for growth cone localization (Figure 4) and radixin interaction (Figure 5C).

claim: Id2 functions downstream of Akt to control axon regrowth.
source: However, co-infection of active Akt with AAV2-Id2-WT significantly enhanced the length and numbers of regenerating axons, suggesting that Id2 functions downstream of Akt, to control axon regrowth (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that active Akt alone is insufficient for axon regrowth but co-infection with Id2 enhances regeneration (Figure 7D, E).

claim: Reactivation of Akt/Id2 signaling after injury in injured CNS neurons may be a useful therapeutic approach for promoting axon regeneration.
source: Thus, our data suggest that reactivation of the Akt/Id2 pathway in injured CNS neurons may be a useful therapeutic approach for promoting axon regeneration.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that AAV2-Id2 infection promotes axon regeneration in injured hippocampal slices (Figure 7).

claim: Reintroduction of Akt/Id2 signaling in injured CNS neurons might be a useful therapeutic approach for promoting axon regeneration.
source: This would suggest that reintroduction of Akt/Id2 signaling in injured CNS neurons might be a useful therapeutic approach for promoting axon regeneration.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the experimental data showing enhanced axon regeneration with AAV2-Id2 and active Akt in injured hippocampal slices (Figure 7D, E).
